title: Informal and Formal Letters
summary: How to write informal and formal letters for Checkpoint 8 Paper 1: British layout, greetings and sign-offs, structure, phrases and two strong 350+ word samples.

blocks.text: 1. What is a letter, and where does it appear?

A **letter** is a piece of writing addressed to one reader (or one organisation) and sent by post. It always has a recognisable **layout**: a greeting at the start, a sign-off at the end, and – depending on the type – addresses and a date at the top. In the Checkpoint 8 exam you meet letters in **Paper 1 (Non-fiction), Section B Writing**, worth **25 marks** with about **35 minutes** suggested. There are two kinds, and you must decide which one the task needs before you write a word.

rows: Who is it to?
Someone you know well: a friend, cousin, grandparent, pen friend.
Someone you do not know personally, or someone in authority: a headteacher, a manager, a council, a company, a newspaper editor.
Purpose
To share news, thank, invite, advise, describe an experience, keep in touch.
To complain, request, apply, suggest, persuade, give an opinion on a public issue.
Tone (register)
Warm, chatty, personal. Contractions (I'm, can't) and light humour are fine.
Polite, serious, precise. No contractions, no slang, no jokes, no emojis.
Greeting
Dear Omar, / Hi Omar,
Dear Sir or Madam, (name unknown) / Dear Mr Saleh, (name known)
Sign-off
Lots of love, / Best wishes, / Take care, + first name only
Yours faithfully, (after Dear Sir or Madam) / Yours sincerely, (after Dear Mr Saleh) + full name

blocks.title: Where letters sit in the exam
items: Paper 1 is Non-fiction: Section A Reading (25 marks) and Section B Writing (25 marks), 1 hour 10 minutes for the whole paper.

A letter can be named directly ("Write a letter to your headteacher…"). Persuasive or complaint letters and formal or informal letters are text types in the framework, so they can appear – but you cannot predict which text type will come in a given series.
Golden rule from the G.A.A.P. technique: only write a letter if the task names a letter. If it names an article or gives no format, do not invent one.

blocks.text: 2. How a letter is marked (out of 25)
Your letter is marked with the same five categories as every Checkpoint writing task. Here is what each band asks for, in simple words, and what it means for a letter.

headers: What the bands ask for (in simple words)
What it means for this genre
rows: Creation of texts (older name: content, purpose and audience)

Bands 1 · 2 · 3 · 4–5. Low: little link to the task. Middle: relevant, some points developed. Top: every point in the task developed in detail, a clear viewpoint, the right tone for the reader all the way through, and the reader stays interested.
Cover every bullet point in the task, in detail. Keep one register from "Dear…" to the sign-off. Show the reader you know who they are (a friend's family, a manager's problem).
Vocabulary and language
1 = simple, repeated words · 2 = some well-chosen words that suit the text type · 3 = precise, ambitious vocabulary chosen for its effect on the reader.
Informal: lively, natural words and idioms (I can't stop grinning). Formal: precise, polite words (express my concern, reconsider, alternatively).
Structure of texts (older name: text structure)

Bands 1 · 2–3 · 4–5 · 6–7. Low: few or no paragraphs. Middle: paragraphs in a sensible order with simple links. Top: well-controlled paragraphs, smooth links between them, an effective opening and ending, and the correct layout for the text type.
Correct layout (address, date, greeting, sign-off), one point per paragraph, an opening that states why you are writing and a closing that asks for a reply or action.
Grammar and punctuation (older name: sentence structure and punctuation)

Bands 1 · 2–3 · 4–5 · 6–7. Low: mostly simple sentences with errors. Middle: some variety, mostly accurate verbs and commas. Top: a wide range of sentence types used for effect, accurate verb forms and a range of punctuation used correctly.
Sentences: mix simple, compound and complex sentences. Punctuation: commas after fronted clauses, apostrophes in contractions (informal), and a semicolon, colon or pair of dashes used correctly.
Word structure (spelling)
1 = many common words wrong · 2 = most common words right · 3 = nearly all words right, including longer, ambitious words.
Spell the letter words correctly: sincerely, faithfully, grateful, convenience, separate, received, recommend.

blocks.title: Three marking rules you must know
items: Wrong text type = heavy penalty. If the task asks for one text type and you write another, Creation of texts is capped at 1 mark and Structure of texts is capped too (at 3, or 2 if the content is also off-task). Layout is not decoration: it protects your marks.
Length: 20 words or fewer scores 0, and 21–60 words can score no more than 7 out of 25. A full answer is several developed paragraphs.
Your plan is not marked. Plan quickly, then spend your time on the writing itself.

blocks.text: Learn the layout features first – they are the easiest marks to protect – then the language features.

rows: Sender's address (top right)
Optional between friends – often just the address or the town.
Always: 15 Lotus Gardens, New Cairo, Cairo (your name does NOT go here).
Date (under your address)
3 June 2026
14 April 2026 (British style: day, month, year)
Recipient's name and address (left side, below the date)
Not used.
The Manager, Riverside Sports Club, 3 Nile View Road, Maadi, Cairo
Greeting (salutation) – on its own line, followed by a comma
Dear Omar,
Dear Sir or Madam, / Dear Mrs Mansour,
Subject line (optional, formal only)
Not used.
Re: Closure of the swimming pool to junior members
Opening paragraph
Ask about the reader, apologise for not writing, say why you are writing.
State your purpose in the first sentence: I am writing to…
Body paragraphs
News and details, one bullet point per paragraph, chatty asides in brackets.
Reasons, evidence and suggestions, one point per paragraph, linked with formal connectives.
Closing paragraph
Ask them to write back and send regards to the family.
Polite request for action + thanks: I look forward to hearing from you.
Sign-off + comma on one line, name on the next line
Lots of love, / Youssef
Yours faithfully, / signature / Karim Adel
Language
Contractions, questions to the reader, exclamations, idioms, humour.
Full forms (I am, do not), formal connectives (Firstly, However, Furthermore), modal verbs for polite requests (could, would).

blocks.title: British conventions examiners notice
items: Dear Sir or Madam (you do not know the name) → Yours faithfully. Memory trick: never put two S words together – Dear Sir … Yours sincerely is wrong.
Dear Mr Saleh / Dear Mrs Mansour / Dear Dr Fahmy (you know the name) → Yours sincerely.
In British English, Mr, Mrs, Ms and Dr are usually written without a full stop. Use the surname, never the first name: Dear Mr Saleh, not Dear Mr Ahmed Saleh or Dear Ahmed.
Capital Y in Yours, small letters in faithfully and sincerely, and a comma after the sign-off.
The greeting and the sign-off each go on their own line; your name goes on the line below the sign-off – first name only for informal letters, full name for formal letters.

blocks.text: Both types follow the same skeleton; only the tone and the content change. Each bullet point in the task normally becomes one body paragraph.

rows: Layout
Your address (optional) and the date, top right.
Your address and the date top right, and the recipient's title/name and address on the left.
Greeting
Dear / Hi / Hello + first name + comma (no comma after Hi itself).
Dear Sir or Madam, or Dear + title + surname + comma. Optional Re: line.
Paragraph 1 – opening
How are you? Mention the reader's life or family, apologise for not writing for so long and give a reason, then say why you are writing now.
Who you are and why you are writing, in one or two sentences: I am writing, as a…, to…
Paragraph 2 – first bullet point
Develop it with details, feelings and an example.
Explain the problem or first point with evidence (numbers, times, examples).
Paragraph 3 – second bullet point
Describe, explain or tell a short story, and add a question to the reader.
Second reason or effect. Show you understand the other side if relevant.
Paragraph 4 – third bullet point
Advice, plans or an invitation.
Your suggestions or solution, clearly and politely.
Closing paragraph
Wrap up warmly, ask for a reply, send regards.
Polite request for action, mention anything enclosed, thank them.
Sign-off
Lots of love, / Best wishes, + first name on the next line.
Yours faithfully, / Yours sincerely, + signature + full name.

items: Read the task and decide: Do I know this person well? → informal. Is it an official person or organisation? → formal.
Underline every bullet point. Each becomes a paragraph.
Decide the greeting and the matching sign-off before you start, so you do not forget.
Write the layout first (address, date, greeting), then the opening paragraph.
Develop each body paragraph with at least three sentences: the point, the detail, the example or feeling.
Finish with a closing paragraph and the correct sign-off.

blocks.text: 5. How to start and how to end

groups.title: Informal openings
items: How are you? I hope you and your family are all well.
I'm so sorry I haven't written for ages; exams have taken over my life!
Thank you so much for your letter – it made my whole week.
You won't believe what happened last weekend!
I've got some amazing news, and you're the first person I wanted to tell.

groups.title: Formal openings
items: I am writing to express my concern about…
I am writing, as a student at…, to request…
I am writing to enquire about…
I would like to bring to your attention a problem that…
I am writing in response to your recent announcement regarding…

groups.title: Informal closings
items: Anyway, I'd better stop before this letter turns into a book!
Write back soon and tell me all your news.
I can't wait to see you – only six weeks to go!
Give my love to everyone at home.
Lots of love, / Best wishes, / Take care, / See you soon,

groups.title: Formal closings
items: I would be grateful if you could consider these suggestions.
I have enclosed… for your reference.
Should you require any further information, please do not hesitate to contact me.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
I look forward to hearing from you at your earliest convenience.

groups.title: Informal: linking and chatting
items: Anyway, back to my news…
By the way, have you heard that…?
Guess what?
Honestly, I couldn't believe it.
You'll never guess who I bumped into…
Oh, and before I forget…

groups.title: Informal: inviting and advising
items: Why don't you come over in the holidays?
How about we…?
If I were you, I'd…
You really must try…
Make sure you bring…

groups.title: Formal: giving reasons
items: Firstly, … Secondly, … Finally, …
Furthermore, / In addition, / Moreover,
As a result, / Consequently,
This is particularly important because…
For example, / For instance,

groups.title: Formal: polite requests and suggestions
items: I would be grateful if you could…
Would it be possible to…?
I would like to suggest that…
Alternatively, the club could…
I fully understand that… However, …
correspondence
letters or emails between people (formal)
enquire / enquiry
to ask for information / a request for information (British spelling)
regarding
about, concerning (formal)
express my concern
say politely that you are worried about something
reconsider
think again about a decision and possibly change it
alternatively
as another possible choice (introduces a second solution)
enclosed
put inside the same envelope: I have enclosed a petition
inconvenience
trouble or difficulty caused to someone
at your earliest convenience
as soon as you can (very formal)
understandably
in a way that is easy to understand – shows you see the other side
catch up
exchange news after a long time (informal)
drop me a line
write to me (informal idiom)
desperate to
wanting something very much (informal, lively)
scorching
extremely hot – stronger than very hot
colossal
extremely large – an ambitious alternative to big

rows: G.A.A.P.: underline the Genre, Audience, Area of content (every bullet point) and Purpose. Decide formal or informal.
Plan: one line per paragraph, plus 3–4 ambitious words and one or two punctuation features you will use.
Write. Keep each bullet point in its own paragraph and develop it with detail, an example or a reason.
Proofread: layout, spelling of ambitious words, capital letters, apostrophes, and the sign-off or ending.

blocks.title: Informal letter: a cousin's visit
blocks.task: Your cousin, who lives in another country, is coming to stay with your family for two weeks in the summer holidays. Write a letter to your cousin. In your letter you should: • say how you feel about the visit • describe two places you will take your cousin and explain why • give advice about what to bring
text: 18 Al-Yasmine Street, Palm Gardens, Cairo
3 June 2026
Dear Omar,

How are you? I hope you, Aunt Salma and the twins are all well, and that the Manchester rain has finally given you a break. I'm really sorry I haven't written for so long; the end-of-year exams swallowed my whole life, and I've only just come up for air. Last night, however, Mum told me the best news of the year, and I had to write straight away: you're coming to stay with us for two whole weeks in August!

Honestly, I can't stop grinning. The last time you visited, we were both eight, and all I can remember is the two of us arguing over the television remote. This time will be completely different. I've already cleared half of my wardrobe for you (a huge sacrifice, believe me), and Dad has promised to take a few days off work so that we can explore properly.

There are two places I'm desperate to show you. The first is the Grand Egyptian Museum, which stands close to the Pyramids of Giza. As soon as you walk in, a colossal statue of Ramesses II towers over you, and then a gigantic staircase lined with ancient kings leads you up towards a window with a view of the pyramids themselves. You love history more than anyone I know, so I'm sure you'll want to spend the whole day there. The second place is Alexandria. We'll take the early train, walk along the Corniche while the sea breeze cools us down, explore the Citadel of Qaitbay and finish with grilled fish at a tiny restaurant my grandfather swears is the best in Egypt.

Before you pack, here's some friendly advice. August in Cairo is scorching – often above 35 degrees – so bring light cotton clothes, a hat, sunscreen and a refillable water bottle. You'll also need comfortable trainers, because we'll be walking for hours, and your swimming things for Alexandria. Oh, and don't forget your football boots: I've told all my friends you're a star striker, so please don't make me a liar!

Anyway, I'd better stop here before this letter turns into a book. Write back soon and tell me what you'd most like to do; I'll make sure it's on our list. Give my love to everyone, and tell the twins I'm saving them a box of my mum's famous basbousa.
Lots of love,
Youssef
blocks.marks: Strong answer — Creation 5/5 · Vocabulary 3/3 · Structure 7/7 · Grammar & punctuation 7/7 · Spelling 3/3
notes: Creation of texts 5/5: all three bullet points are covered and developed – feelings (paragraph 2), two places with reasons (paragraph 3), advice on packing (paragraph 4). The writer knows the reader (Aunt Salma, the twins, Omar's love of history), which builds a real writer–reader relationship.
Vocabulary 3/3: lively, precise word choices that suit a friend – swallowed my whole life, come up for air, colossal, towers over you, scorching, desperate.

Structure 7/7: correct informal layout (address and date top right, Dear Omar, on its own line, Lots of love, + first name on the next line). The opening asks about the reader, apologises for not writing and gives a reason. Each body paragraph handles one bullet point, and the closing asks for a reply. Links between paragraphs: This time will be completely different… / Before you pack… / Anyway…

Grammar & punctuation – sentences: a range of sentence types – a short simple sentence for effect (Honestly, I can't stop grinning.), compound sentences and complex sentences (As soon as you walk in, a colossal statue…).

Grammar & punctuation – punctuation: accurate apostrophes in contractions, a colon for explanation (I had to write straight away: you're coming…), a semicolon joining two related sentences (…for so long; the end-of-year exams…), brackets for extra information, and a pair of dashes for extra information (– often above 35 degrees –). Together these earn 7/7.
Spelling 3/3: ambitious words spelt correctly – sacrifice, colossal, gigantic, refillable, restaurant, grandfather, comfortable.
Note: the address and date are shown on single lines here; in the exam, write each part of the address on its own line in the top-right corner, with the date underneath.

blocks.title: Formal letter: a complaint with suggestions
blocks.task: Your local sports club has announced that its swimming pool will be closed to members under sixteen on weekday evenings. Write a letter to the manager of the club. In your letter you should: • explain why this decision is a problem for young members • describe how it affects others • suggest a fairer solution
text: 15 Lotus Gardens, New Cairo, Cairo
14 April 2026
The Manager, Riverside Sports Club, 3 Nile View Road, Maadi, Cairo
Dear Sir or Madam,
Re: Closure of the swimming pool to junior members on weekday evenings

I am writing, as a junior member of Riverside Sports Club for the past five years, to express my concern about the recent announcement that the swimming pool will be closed to members under sixteen between 5 p.m. and 9 p.m., Sunday to Thursday, from next month.

Firstly, this decision would make it almost impossible for young people to swim during the week. Most of us finish school at half past three and attend lessons or complete homework until five, so the evening is the only time we can train. The club's junior swimming team, which has won three regional medals this year alone, trains on exactly these evenings. If the new timetable goes ahead, the team will lose four of its five weekly sessions – and, very probably, its best swimmers.

Secondly, the closure affects far more than competitions. Swimming is one of the few activities that keeps teenagers active without the pressure of exams; it is also a skill that can save lives. Parents pay a full family membership on the understanding that every member, regardless of age, can use the facilities. Several families I have spoken to feel, quite understandably, that they would no longer be receiving the service they have paid for.

I fully understand that adult members have complained about crowded lanes in the evenings, and I agree that the pool can become uncomfortably busy. However, I believe there are fairer solutions. The club could reserve two lanes for juniors and the remaining lanes for adults; alternatively, junior members could be given three evenings a week instead of none. A supervised junior session from 5 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. would also keep the pool calmer for adults later in the evening.

I would be grateful if you could reconsider this decision before it takes effect. I have enclosed a petition signed by sixty-three junior members and their parents, and I would be happy to meet you, together with our swimming coach, to discuss these suggestions in more detail.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to hearing from you at your earliest convenience.
Yours faithfully,
(signature)
Karim Adel
blocks.marks: Strong answer — Creation 5/5 · Vocabulary 3/3 · Structure 7/7 · Grammar & punctuation 7/7 · Spelling 3/3
notes: Creation of texts 5/5: every bullet point has its own developed paragraph – the problem (paragraph 2), the wider effects (paragraph 3), fair solutions (paragraph 4). The viewpoint is clear but reasonable, and the writer shows understanding of the club's side (I fully understand that adult members have complained…), which persuades a formal reader.
Vocabulary 3/3: precise formal vocabulary – express my concern, regardless of age, quite understandably, reconsider, alternatively, enclosed, at your earliest convenience.

Structure 7/7: full British formal layout – sender's address and date, recipient's title and address, Dear Sir or Madam, a Re: subject line, and Yours faithfully, followed by the full name. The opening states who is writing and why in one sentence. Firstly, Secondly and However guide the reader, and the closing asks for action and thanks the reader.

Grammar & punctuation – sentences: no contractions anywhere, varied complex sentences (If the new timetable goes ahead, the team will lose…), a relative clause (…team, which has won three regional medals this year alone, trains…) and modal verbs for polite suggestions (could, would).

Grammar & punctuation – punctuation: a semicolon joining two related sentences (…without the pressure of exams; it is also a skill…), pairs of commas for extra information (feel, quite understandably, that…) and a single dash for emphasis (– and, very probably, its best swimmers). Together these earn 7/7.
Spelling 3/3: faithfully, convenience, consideration, petition, regional, understandably, alternatively – all correct.
Note: Dear Sir or Madam → Yours faithfully. If the task gave the manager's name, the letter would open Dear Mr Hassan, and close Yours sincerely,.

rows: Dear Sir or Madam … Yours sincerely
Wrong convention – a structure and accuracy slip a marker spots at once.
Unknown name → faithfully. Known name → sincerely.
Mixing registers: I'm writing to complain… Cheers!
Creation of texts needs a consistent tone for the reader.
Choose formal or informal at the start and keep it to the end.
Hi, Omar, (a comma after Hi) or Dear Omar on the same line as the first sentence
Layout error.
No comma after Hi itself: Hi Omar, or Dear Omar, on its own line, then start the letter on the next line.
Sign-off and name on the same line, or your full name in an informal letter
Layout error.
Sign-off + comma on one line, then the name below: first name only for friends.
Skipping one bullet point
Creation of texts cannot reach the top band.
Tick each bullet point on the question paper as you write its paragraph.
One-sentence paragraphs that only mention the point
Ideas are not developed.
Point + detail + example or feeling – at least three sentences.
Writing your own name in the address
Not British convention.
The address shows only the street, area and city.
Contractions or slang in a formal letter (don't, kids, stuff)
Wrong register lowers Creation and Vocabulary.
Use full forms and formal words: do not, children, equipment.

items: I chose the right type (formal/informal) for the reader named in the task.
Address and date are top right; for a formal letter, the recipient's address is on the left.
Greeting + comma on its own line. Sign-off + comma on its own line, with my name below it.
Sir or Madam → Yours faithfully. A named person → Yours sincerely.
Every bullet point has its own developed paragraph.
The register is the same from the first line to the last.
I used at least three sentence types (simple, compound, complex).
I used at least one of: a semicolon joining two related sentences, a colon, a pair of dashes, brackets.
I checked the spelling of sincerely, faithfully, grateful and every ambitious word.

blocks.title: كيف تحصل على الدرجة النهائية في الخطاب
items: الخطوة الأولى: حدِّد هل الخطاب رسمي (إلى مدير أو شركة أو مجلس) أم غير رسمي (إلى صديق أو قريب)، لأن اللغة والتحية والختام تتغير حسب ذلك.
إذا بدأت بـ Dear Sir or Madam فاختم بـ Yours faithfully، وإذا كتبت اسم الشخص (Dear Mr Saleh) فاختم بـ Yours sincerely.
اكتب التحية في سطر مستقل وبعدها فاصلة، والختام في سطر مستقل وبعده فاصلة، ثم اسمك في السطر التالي.
كل نقطة في السؤال = فقرة كاملة فيها تفاصيل ومثال. إذا نسيت نقطة فلن تصل إلى أعلى مستوى في درجة المحتوى.
لا تستخدم الاختصارات مثل (I'm – don't) في الخطاب الرسمي.

items.q: Task A (informal): Your best friend has just moved to a new school in another city. Write a letter to your friend. You should: • tell them your news from your class • ask about their new school • suggest a plan for the next holiday. Write a quick plan.
items.a: Plan – Layout: address + date top right, Dear Karim, → Lots of love, / Best wishes, + first name. P1: How are you? Sorry for not writing sooner (football tournament). Writing because I miss you. P2: class news – new science teacher, the class trip to the Fayoum desert, a funny moment. P3: questions about the new school – friends, teachers, is the food better than ours? P4: holiday plan – you stay with us for a week in the mid-year break, with cycling in the park, a football match. P5: write back soon, regards to your parents. Words to use: hilarious, unforgettable, I can't wait. Punctuation: brackets for an aside, a semicolon joining two related sentences.

items.q: Task B (formal): Your town council plans to turn the only public park in your area into a car park. Write a letter to the head of the council, Mr Tarek Shawky. You should: • explain why the park matters to local people • describe what would be lost • suggest an alternative. Which greeting and sign-off do you use, and what goes in each paragraph?
items.a: Greeting: Dear Mr Shawky, → Yours sincerely, (the name is known), then your full name. Layout: your address and date top right. Mr Tarek Shawky, Head of … Council, address on the left. Re: Proposed car park on … Park. P1: I am writing, as a resident of …, to express my concern about… P2: why it matters – the only green space, children, elderly people walking, clean air. P3: what would be lost – trees, the playground, community events, plus one number for evidence. P4: alternatives – a multi-storey car park on the empty land near the market, or better bus services. P5: I would be grateful if you could reconsider… I look forward to hearing from you.

items.q: Correct the layout errors: "Hi Omar, how are you? … Love Youssef Ahmed."
items.a: Hi Omar, (or Dear Omar,) on its own line, then How are you? on the next line. The ending should be: Love, (with a comma, on its own line) and then Youssef on the line below – first name only in an informal letter.

items.q: A student writes: "Dear Sir or Madam, I'm writing cos the pool is closed and it's so unfair!!! Yours sincerely, Karim." Give four corrections.
items.a: 1) I'm → I am, and cos → because (formal register, no contractions or slang). 2) so unfair!!! → one polite, precise statement, e.g. I believe this decision is unfair to junior members. (no multiple exclamation marks). 3) Yours sincerely → Yours faithfully, because the letter starts Dear Sir or Madam. 4) Karim → full name, Karim Adel, on the line below the sign-off.
